requirements.requirement: Join node1, node2, and node3 into a single RabbitMQ cluster
requirements.summary: node2 and node3 joined node1 as disc nodes via rabbitmqctl join_cluster; cluster_status directly confirms all three nodes running with no partitions.

requirements.requirement: Create a payments virtual host and an application account that can publish and consume there
requirements.summary: payments vhost and app_user created with configure/write/read '.*' permissions scoped to payments; app_user credentials were subsequently used successfully to declare a queue, publish messages, and consume messages via rabbitmqadmin, directly demonstrating publish/consume capability.

requirements.requirement: Messages published to a durable queue must survive the loss of any one node and stay consumable from the remaining nodes
requirements.summary: A durable queue 'orders' with ha-all/automatic mirroring was declared and 3 persistent messages published (delivery_mode=2), with synchronised_slave_pids confirming mirrors on node2 and node3. Node1 (the queue master) was then stopped via rabbitmqctl stop_app; cluster_status from node2 showed the remaining two nodes running with the queue mirrored, and all 3 messages were successfully retrieved via rabbitmqadmin get from node2 while node1 remained down. This is a direct, observed baseline -> disruption -> consumption transition, not just configuration.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task contract are satisfied with direct evidence: a 3-node cluster was formed, a payments vhost with a working application account (app_user) was created, and durability under node loss was directly demonstrated — a durable, HA-mirrored queue with 3 persistent messages remained intact and fully consumable from node2 after node1 (the queue master) was stopped. The independent provider-wide restart protocol was also completed on all three nodes with clear pre-restart baselines, restart acknowledgements, changed boot identities (cross-checked against the fixed after_executor snapshot), and confirmed post-restart recovery of cluster membership, vhost, policy, and queue state, plus a final end-to-end publish/consume check. Hygiene is high; the only residue is a small, low-risk rabbitmqadmin helper script left in /tmp on node1.
limitations: The executor's own evidence-selection report cites a command ID (cmd-da9c48f5d441f9) that does not exist in the timeline; the actual command performing that action is cmd-da5d9c48f5d441f9 — a clerical mismatch, not a gap in the underlying evidence.

Message content/count was not re-verified inside the queue after the full restart cycle, but this is expected since all messages had already been drained during the node-loss durability test before restarts began, so it does not weaken the durability finding.
Executor evidence item 3 referenced unknown command IDs: cmd-da9c48f5d441f9

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were almost entirely diagnostic, required setup, or evidence collection. One small leftover file (/tmp/rabbitmqadmin, a helper CLI script fetched over HTTP with basic auth from the local RabbitMQ management API) persists on node1 in the after_executor snapshot; it is a low-risk, non-sensitive script needed to run rabbitmqadmin without pika, and was re-downloaded (cmd-a0e547a1511c41c2) after the reboot wiped the first copy (whose absence caused the earlier failed attempt cmd-5a96587e32814d26). Two failed rabbitmqadmin invocations on node2 (cmd-963be4f07ee44bab, cmd-efcb531ad5924325) were argument-syntax trial-and-error while discovering the correct 'get' flags, not state-changing mutations, and were corrected in the same sequence (cmd-bb5c4e2eb849464c). A failed pika import check (cmd-16c8971e52674f0d) was read-only diagnostics. No failed services, package inconsistency, unsafe exposure, or unreverted destructive changes are visible in the after_executor snapshots.
